title: A literate FizzBuzz
summary: A bag that holds a code block is a named chunk, and a line holding only <<<name>>> links to it. That is how the original barkdown labels code, and it…
text: A bag that holds a code block is a named chunk, and a line holding only <<<name>>> links to it. That is how the original barkdown labels code, and it turns a post into a small literate program. Follow the link in the first block. The program counts from 1 to 100. go func main() { for i := 1; i <= 100; i++ { <<<print one number>>> } } Multiples of 15 are tested first, because they are also multiples of 3 and of 5. go switch { case i%15 == 0: fmt.Println("FizzBuzz") case i%3 == 0: fmt.Println("Fizz") case i%5 == 0: fmt.Println("Buzz") default: fmt.Println(i) }

title: A tour of barkdown
summary: Every tag barkdown understands, shown in use.
text: Programs must be written for people to read, and only incidentally for machines to execute. Harold Abelson and Gerald Jay Sussman, Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs This post shows what a barkdown post can contain. Its source is posts/2026-11-03-tour/index.bt; read the two side by side. Text Paragraphs are separated by blank lines. Inside them you can write bold, italic, emphasis, inline code or inline code, highlights, struck text, H2O, E = mc2, keys like Ctrl + C, and abbreviations such as HyperText Markup Language. A line breakgoes like this. The characters #, {, } and backticks go between backticks. Links take the URL first: the brashtag repository. Links to other posts use their slug, like , and are checked when the site is built. A URL with a fragment goes between backticks: learning Go. Let us change our traditional attitude to the construction of programs: Instead of imagining that our main task is to instruct a computer what to do, let us concentrate rather on explaining to human beings what we want a computer to do. Donald E. Knuth, Literate Programming Lists - Each line is an item. - A line may start with a dash, as in Markdown. - A nested list sits on a line of its own. - Items can hold markup and code, with commas. First Second Third The comma separated list of the original barkdown still works, and like every list it is a block of its own: one, two, three Tables Language | Typing | First appeared --- | --- | --- Go | static | 2009 Python | dynamic | 1991 Cells are separated by pipes; a row of dashes makes the row above it a header. Code go package main import "fmt" // main says hello. func main() { fmt.Println("Hello, barkdown", 42) } python def fib(n): """Return the n-th Fibonacci number.""" a, b = 0, 1 for _ in range(n): a, b = b, a + b return a sh # build the site and publish it barkdown build -strict && rsync -a public/ "$HOST:/var/www/site/" bt #title{A post} Some text with `#code` and a #b{bold} word. Notes and asides Notes are written in placeLike this one. It sits in the margin, level with the line that mentions it. and numbered automaticallyOn a phone there is no margin, so the number becomes a button: tap it to read the note.. A margin note has no number.A margin note is for a remark or a caption that needs no reference mark. A change of subject that does not deserve a heading can open with small capitals instead. Call-outs come in six kinds: note, tip, info, warning, danger and important. A custom title A title bag inside a call-out replaces its label. A stray } in prose ends the document early. Barkdown reports the line. Click to see more This stays hidden until the reader asks for it. Figures How barkdown works: a post is parsed into a tree, and the tree is rendered as HTML. The image lives next to the post, in its bundle. Math and diagrams Inline math is code between dollar signs: $e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0$. Display math uses a bag: \sum_{k=1}^{n} k = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} Diagrams are Mermaid code blocks: mermaid graph LR A[post.bt] --> B[brashtag tree] --> C[HTML page] Raw HTML

title: Notes on margins
summary: Thoughts on margins as they come to me while building this site's theme. They will keep arriving. Tufte's books keep a wide margin on every page, and use it: notes,…
text: Thoughts on margins as they come to me while building this site's theme. They will keep arriving. Tufte's books keep a wide margin on every page, and use it: notes, small pictures, captions. The margin is not empty space waiting for something; it is where the second voice of the book lives. A footnote asks the reader to leave the line and come back. A sidenote waits beside it.This one, for instance. The difference sounds small and is not. On a phone there is no margin, so the notes fold away behind their numbers. Tufte CSS does this with a hidden checkbox and no script at all, which is the kind of trick worth keeping. Code wants a margin too: the language of a listing, its name in a literate program, a button to copy it. None of these is part of the code, so none of them should sit on top of it.

title: Welcome to barkdown
summary: This is the first post of a site made with barkdown. Posts are written in brashtag: plain text, with #tag{...} bags where structure is needed. Write a paragraph, leave a…
text: This is the first post of a site made with barkdown. Posts are written in brashtag: plain text, with #tag{...} bags where structure is needed. Write a paragraph, leave a blank line, write the next one. That is most of it. Everything above the #more{} marker is the excerpt shown on the home page. The rest appears only on the post's own page. Next steps Run barkdown serve and open the address it prints. Edit this file and watch the browser reload. Read for every tag barkdown understands. Run barkdown build and copy public/ to any static host.

title: About

text: This site was made by barkdown init. Replace its files with your own: - site.bt holds the settings. - posts/ holds the posts, newest first on the home page. - pages/ holds pages like this one, which appear in the menu. - static/ is copied to the site as it is. - templates/ may override any part of the theme. See for everything a post can contain.
